title: Relative clauses II: vilket, det som, allt som
title_target: Det som jag gillar mest är att havet aldrig är långt borta.
goal: Say "what", "everything that", "the one who" and "which" the Swedish way — and link a comment to a whole sentence with *vilket*.
bekal: you can use *det som*, *allt som* and *den som* where English says "what", "everything that" and "the one who"
you can add *som* in indirect questions when the question word is the subject (*vem som ringde*)
you can comment on a whole statement with *vilket* and recognize formal *vilken/vilket/vilka* after prepositions
wave: Go back to Unit 4: take five of its direct questions, turn each into an indirect one (*Vem ringde?* → *Jag vet inte vem som ringde*), and mark every case where the question word is the subject and therefore needs *som*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kunden som vet vad hon vill
dialogs.intro: Monday morning at the design studio in Göteborg. A client has sent an unhappy email over the weekend, and Mattias explains to Dian what it's all about.

lines.text: Ja, men jag förstod inte riktigt vad som var fel.
lines.id: Yes, but I didn't really understand what was wrong.
lines.literal: yes, but I understood not really what that was wrong.

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Det som stör dem är färgerna. De vill ha något som känns mer Göteborg.

notes: **vad som var fel** — when you turn a question into an indirect one and the question word is the **subject**, Swedish inserts *som*: *Vad var fel?* → *jag förstod inte vad **som** var fel*; *Vem skrev mejlet?* → *vet du vem **som** skrev mejlet?* Leaving *som* out here is one of the clearest signs of a foreign accent in writing. When the question word is the **object**, there is no *som*: *en kund som vet vad hon vill* (she wants *what*).

**Det som stör dem är färgerna** — English starts with "What bothers them…", but Swedish cannot use *vad* here. It says *det som*, literally "that which". *Vad stör dem är färgerna* is a classic learner mistake; train your ear on *det som* until it feels automatic.

**allt jag har samlat** — just like plain *som* (Svenska 102, Unit 13), *som* after *allt* and *det* may be dropped when it is not the subject of its clause: *allt (som) jag har samlat*, *det (som) hon ber om*. It must stay when it is the subject: *allt **som** kan gå fel*.

**vilket de tyckte var för tråkigt** — *vilket* (**VIL-ket**) points back to the **whole** previous statement, like English ", which…". *Som* can never do this job, and the form is always *vilket*, whatever the gender of the nouns nearby. Mattias uses it again a moment later: *vilket betyder att vi har fyra dagar*.

**den som bestämmer** — *den som* means "the one who" or "whoever"; the plural is *de som* (**dom som**), "those who". *Den som väntar på något gott väntar aldrig för länge* — good things come to those who wait.

**vars namn** (**vahsh nahmn**) means "whose". You met it in Svenska 102; at B1 you'll see it constantly in written Swedish. In speech many Swedes rephrase instead: *mappen som heter Ref-något*. And **kolla** (**KOL-lah**, to check, to look) is the everyday word — *kontrollera* belongs to forms and manuals.

grammars.title: Det som, allt som, den som, vad som
body: English packs many meanings into "what" and "who". Swedish splits them up. The left column is the English you want to say; the middle column is the Swedish that does it.

head: English
Swedish
Example
rows: Han vet **vilka ställen som** är bäst.

after: The rule for dropping *som* is the same everywhere: you may drop it when something else in the clause is the subject (*det jag vill*, *allt hon sa*), never when *som* itself is the subject (*det som hände*).
Three handy fixed phrases are built the same way: **vad som helst** (anything at all), **vem som helst** (anyone at all), **var som helst** (anywhere at all). *Du kan sitta var som helst.*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Lunch vid älven
dialogs.intro: Dian and Leila eat their lunch boxes on a bench by the Göta älv river, near the office. Leila wants to know how Dian is getting on in her new city.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Hur trivs du i Göteborg nu, när du har bott här ett tag?
lines.id: How do you like Göteborg now that you've lived here for a while?
lines.literal: how thrive you in Göteborg now, when you have lived here a while?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jättebra! Det som jag gillar mest är att havet aldrig är långt borta.
lines.id: I love it! What I like most is that the sea is never far away.
lines.literal: giant-good! that which I like most is that sea-the never is far away.

lines.literal: no, trams-the. mine was late three times last week, which Karin not thought was so fun.

lines.literal: all that can go wrong with trams-the goes wrong. that know all here.

lines.text: Vad heter förresten gatan som du pratade om, den med alla kaféer?

lines.text: Andra Långgatan. Där finns allt som en student behöver: billig mat, vintage och bra musik.

lines.literal: Second Long-street-the. there exists all that a student needs: cheap food, vintage and good music.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Perfekt. Det är precis vad jag behöver efter en sådan vecka.

lines.literal: perfect. it is exactly what I need after a such week.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Vi kan gå dit på fredag, vilket passar bra eftersom vi ändå slutar tidigt.

lines.literal: we can go there on Friday, which suits well since we anyway finish early.

lines.text: Gärna! Fråga Mattias också, om han vill hänga med.
lines.id: I'd love to! Ask Mattias too, if he wants to come along.
lines.literal: gladly! ask Mattias also, if he wants hang with.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Han säger nog ja. Han är den som alltid vet vilka ställen som är bäst.
lines.id: He'll probably say yes. He's the one who always knows which places are best.
lines.literal: he says probably yes. he is the-one that always knows which places that are best.

notes: **Hur trivs du?** — *trivas* (to be happy somewhere, to feel at home) is one of those *-s* verbs you met in Svenska 102. *Hur trivs du?* is the standard way to ask how someone likes a new city, job or apartment, and *Jag trivs jättebra* is the standard happy answer.

**vilket Karin inte tyckte var så kul** — a clause with *vilket* is a subordinate clause, so the BIFF rule applies: *inte* comes **before** the verb. The same is true after *som*, *det som* and *allt som*: *det som inte fungerar*, *allt som jag inte förstår*.

**gatan som du pratade om** — the preposition goes to the **end** of the clause, just as in casual English ("the street you were talking about"). Swedish never puts a preposition in front of *som*: *gatan om som…* is impossible. In formal writing you'll instead see *gatan om vilken du talade* — see the grammar box below.

**vilka ställen som är bäst** — the *som* rule from the first dialogue again: *vilka ställen* is the subject of *är bäst*, so *som* follows. Compare *jag vet vilka ställen du gillar*, where *du* is the subject and no *som* is needed.

**Andra Långgatan** (**AHN-drah LONG-gah-tahn**), "Second Long Street", is Göteborg's bohemian street in the Linné district, which locals simply call *Långgatorna*. **Älven** (**EL-ven**) — "the river" — is what Göteborgers call the Göta älv, the river that runs out into the sea right through the city.
**hänga med** (**heng-ah MEHD**) means "to come along" — and also "to keep up, to follow": *Hänger du med?* (Are you with me? / Are you coming?). It's a particle verb, so the stress falls on *med*.

grammars.title: Vilken, vilket, vilka as relative words
body: **Job 1 — commenting on a whole statement.** Here only *vilket* is possible, and it is common in both speech and writing: *Spårvagnen var sen, **vilket** gjorde Karin irriterad.* If you can replace it with "and that" (*och det gjorde Karin irriterad*), *vilket* is right.

**Job 2 — a formal replacement for *som*.** In written, rather formal Swedish, *vilken* (en-word), *vilket* (ett-word) and *vilka* (plural) can replace *som*, agreeing with the noun they refer to. Today this is used almost only **after a preposition**, because *som* can't follow one. In speech, use *som* and move the preposition to the end.
after: Never use *vilket* for a single noun in everyday speech: *huset vilket vi köpte* sounds stiff. With a whole statement, though, *vilket* is the only choice.
In very formal texts you may also meet *vari* (in which), *varav* (of which) and *varpå* (whereupon). Recognize them; there's no need to use them yet.

blocks.text: By now you have a whole toolkit for linking information to a noun. Most of the time **som** is all you need. The others each do one special job.

Job
Example

Det regnade, **vilket** ingen var förvånad över.

blocks.text: **Där** and **dit** follow the same split as *här/hit* and *var/vart*: *där* for being somewhere, *dit* for going there. *Staden dit vi åkte* (the city we went to), *staden där vi bodde* (the city where we lived).

blocks.title: Three mistakes to stop making now
items: *Vad jag vill är att sova.* → **Det** jag vill är att sova. ("What" at the start of a sentence is *det som* / *det*.)
*Jag vet inte vem ringde.* → Jag vet inte vem **som** ringde. (Question word = subject → add *som*.)
*Han kom sent, som gjorde mig arg.* → Han kom sent, **vilket** gjorde mig arg. (A whole statement → *vilket*.)

blocks.text: Göteborg is Sweden's second city, a port town of about 600,000 people that feels smaller and friendlier than Stockholm. Its public transport is run by **Västtrafik**, and its backbone is the tram network — the largest in Scandinavia.

blocks.text: Locals have their own word for anything nice: **gött** (**yött**), roughly "lovely, great" — *Vad gött!* It is the Göteborg version of *skönt*, and you'll hear it from the first day. You'll learn more about Göteborg speech in Svenska 104.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Svenska 102, Unit 13
items: Describe five people in your life with one *som*-clause each: *Elin är en vän som jobbar på ett bibliotek.*
Now drop *som* wherever you're allowed to: *en film (som) jag har sett*, but *en vän som jobbar…*
Finally add one *vilket* comment to each: *Hon jobbar på helgerna, vilket jag inte skulle orka.*
